subsystem: usvfs NT/Win32 API hooking layer (path interception + rewrite) vs. Eidos FUSE union
whatMo2Does:
usvfs is a DLL injected into the game (and every child process) that trampoline-patches ~30 functions in ntdll.dll, kernel32.dll/kernelbase.dll. The architecture has four pillars:

1. REDIRECTION TREE (the index). A `RedirectionTree` lives in boost interprocess shared memory (`m_Tree`, 4 MiB; plus a 128 KiB `m_InverseTree`). It is populated up-front from the mod stack via `usvfsVirtualLinkFile`/`usvfsVirtualLinkDirectoryStatic` (usvfs.cpp), each tree node mapping a virtual game-dir path -> a real on-disk file (`linkTarget`) with flags (FLAG_DIRECTORY, FLAG_CREATETARGET = "writes land here", FLAG_DUMMY). This is the in-memory resolver MO2 builds before launch.

2. REROUTE ENGINE (maptracker.h). `RerouteW::create` canonicalizes the incoming path (`absolutePath` strips \??\/\\?\, resolves relative against CWD; `canonizePath` lexically normalizes), looks it up in the tree via `findNode`, and if found rewrites the path string to the real target. `CreateRerouter::rerouteCreate` additionally maps Win32 dispositions (CREATE_NEW/OPEN_ALWAYS/TRUNCATE...) to decide read-vs-create, and on create-of-new-file picks the deepest FLAG_CREATETARGET ancestor (overwrite dir) via `visitPath`, materializing a "fake" parent path with `createFakePath` (tracked in `k32FakeDirTracker` so it can be cleaned up). Deletions are tracked in `k32DeleteTracker` so a recreated deleted file reroutes back to its overwrite location.

3. WHAT EACH HOOK REWRITES:
   - NtCreateFile/NtOpenFile (ntdll.cpp): build a UnicodeString from `ObjectAttributes` (RootDirectory handle via `ntdllHandleTracker` + ObjectName), reroute it, then `makeObjectAttributes` clones OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES with `RootDirectory=nullptr` and `ObjectName=` the rewritten `\??\`-prefixed path, and calls the real function. NtCreateFile also converts disposition both ways and inserts the new mapping into the tree on success.
   - NtQueryAttributesFile / NtQueryFullAttributesFile / NtQueryInformationByName: reroute the OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES path, call real (these answer file-exists/size/timestamps before any open).
   - NtQueryDirectoryFile / NtQueryDirectoryFileEx (the most complex, ~150 lines each): MERGE a directory. `gatherVirtualEntries` collects tree nodes mapped into this dir; then it enumerates the REAL directory and emits entries, building a `foundFiles` upper-cased skip-set; then appends the virtual entries that weren't already present. Per-search state (`Searches::Info`: foundFiles set, currentSearchHandle, virtualMatches queue) is keyed by the directory HANDLE in `HookContext::customData`.
   - NtQueryInformationFile (FileNameInformation/FileNormalizedNameInformation/FileAllInformation), NtQueryObject (ObjectNameInformation): REVERSE rewrite — when the game asks "what's the path of this handle?", usvfs looks up the handle's tracked path, reroutes it, and rewrites the returned name back to the VIRTUAL path (NtQueryObject even re-derives the device name via QueryDosDeviceW). This is module-path spoofing.
   - kernel32 wrappers: GetFileAttributes[Ex]W (+ A->W thunks), SetFileAttributesW, DeleteFileW, CreateDirectoryW, RemoveDirectoryW, MoveFile*/CopyFile*/CopyFile2, GetPrivateProfileString/Section + WritePrivateProfileString (INI redirection), GetFullPathNameW, FindFirstFileExW, SetCurrentDirectory/GetCurrentDirectory (CWD tracked per-drive in `k32CurrentDirectoryTracker`), GetModuleFileName[AW] (reverse rewrite using the INVERSE tree), LoadLibraryEx[AW] (reroute the DLL path), CreateProcessInternalW (reroute the exe, force CREATE_SUSPENDED, INJECT usvfs into the child via `injectProcess`, then resume — this is how the VFS propagates to child processes/tools), ExitProcess/NtTerminateProcess (disconnect VFS).

4. DISPATCH + CALL CONTEXT. `HookManager::installHook` resolves each symbol (`MyGetProcAddress`) and installs a trampoline. Every hook body is wrapped in HOOK_START_GROUP(group)/HOOK_END macros: a thread-local `HookStack` holds a bitset of active `MutExHookGroup`s (OPEN_FILE, FIND_FILES, FILE_ATTRIBUTES, SHELL_FILEOP...). `HookCallContext(group)` sets the group bit; if already set (`!callContext.active()`), the hook calls straight through to the real function. This is a RE-ENTRANCY guard: a hook that internally calls another hooked Win32 API (e.g. reroute calling GetFileAttributesW) won't recursively re-trigger same-group rewriting. ALL_GROUPS blocks everything. `PreserveGetLastError`/PRE_REALCALL/POST_REALCALL carefully save and restore GetLastError across the rewrite work so the game sees the real call's error. SKIP LISTS: `interestingPath` rejects \\.\ device specs and "hid#"; `isDeviceFile` passes \Device\ paths straight through; per-file-suffix and per-directory skip lists are consumed at TREE-POPULATION time (`fileNameInSkipSuffixes`/`fileNameInSkipDirectories` in usvfs.cpp), not per call. Forced libraries (`librariesToForceLoad`) are LoadLibrary'd at init.
whyItMatters: This hooking layer IS usvfs — it is the entire mechanism MO2 exists to provide. The question "what does Eidos need to replicate" is answered by enumerating these hooks. The crucial finding is that hooking and a FUSE-under-Wine mount are two implementations of the SAME abstraction (intercept a path operation, rewrite/merge it), but at different layers: usvfs intercepts ABOVE Wine (inside the Windows process, at the Win32/NT boundary), Eidos intercepts BELOW Wine (at the Linux VFS, after Wine has already translated the NT call into a host syscall). Understanding which usvfs behaviors are intrinsic to the union abstraction (and therefore handled for free by any correct union FS) versus which are Windows-API artifacts (and therefore either irrelevant or must be re-created elsewhere) is what tells Eidos where its remaining work is. Getting this wrong in either direction wastes effort: re-implementing per-call rewriting that Wine already does, or missing the handful of behaviors that genuinely have no VFS equivalent and will silently break specific mods/tools.
eidosCurrentState:
Eidos already implements the union abstraction natively and correctly, which is exactly the behavior MOST usvfs hooks deliver:

- eidos-core/src/lib.rs `LayerStack` is the analog of the RedirectionTree + RerouteW combined: `resolve_read` (overwrite-shadows-everything, then mod layers in priority order, then game), `resolve_write`/`open_for_write` (copy-up into Overwrite = usvfs's FLAG_CREATETARGET behavior), `remove` (whiteout markers `.eidoswh.<name>` = usvfs's k32DeleteTracker), `rename`, `list_dir` (the merge that NtQueryDirectoryFile does, deduped case-insensitively, NTFS-sorted). Case-insensitivity is `eq_ignore_case`/`ci_lookup` (ASCII fold, exactly matching usvfs's `_strnicmp` tree). This is unit-tested (~20 tests).
- eidos-fuse/src/lib.rs `Eidos` translates VFS ops (lookup/getattr/readdir/open/read/write/create/mkdir/unlink/rename/setattr/symlink/xattr/statfs) onto LayerStack. Wine maps NtCreateFile->open, NtQueryDirectoryFile->getdents64, NtQueryAttributesFile->stat, NtQueryInformationFile->fstat/readlink, etc., so all those usvfs hooks are covered IMPLICITLY by the kernel routing the host syscall to this FUSE daemon. xattr passthrough (user.DOSATTRIB) covers Set/GetFileAttributes. Kernel passthrough (FUSE_PASSTHROUGH) covers DLL image-mapping (the LoadLibraryEx concern) — validated: ~50 SKSE plugins load.
- eidos-launch/src/lib.rs enters a user+mount namespace and runs the game with CWD=game-root. This is the analog of usvfs's per-process scope + CWD handling — but achieved by namespace isolation, so it is automatically inherited by every CHILD process (no per-process DLL injection needed). This already covers the CreateProcessInternalW injection's PURPOSE for the game's own subprocesses.

NO Eidos code anywhere touches: module-path spoofing, an inverse tree, per-call skip lists, handle tracking, or tools-through-VFS re-entry (grep confirms zero hits). The architecture.md doc acknowledges rename-across-lower-boundary and Unicode casefold as known gaps, and frames re-entry for tools (xEdit/FNIS) as a wrapper requirement that "must be able to re-enter the namespace" — but it is NOT yet built.
eidosGap:
Mapping every usvfs hook to Eidos, three behaviors have NO FUSE equivalent and are genuinely missing; the rest are covered or irrelevant:

COVERED IMPLICITLY by the FUSE union (Wine translates the NT call to a host syscall that hits the mount): NtCreateFile, NtOpenFile, NtQueryAttributesFile, NtQueryFullAttributesFile, NtQueryInformationByName, NtQueryDirectoryFile/Ex (the merge — Eidos `list_dir`), GetFileAttributes*, SetFileAttributes (xattr), Delete/CreateDirectory/RemoveDirectory, MoveFile*/CopyFile* (Wine issues rename/open+read+write through the mount; Eidos `rename`+COW handle it), GetPrivateProfileString/WritePrivateProfileString (INIs are just file reads/writes), FindFirstFileExW (-> opendir/readdir), Get/SetCurrentDirectory (namespace + CWD), NtClose (Eidos `release`/`forget`).

IRRELEVANT under Wine: the `MutExHookGroup` re-entrancy guard, `HookCallContext`/PreserveGetLastError (these exist only because hooks run IN-process and call other hooked APIs — a FUSE daemon has no such reentrancy), `isDeviceFile`/`interestingPath` \\.\ \Device\ hid# filtering (those never reach a host file mount; Wine routes devices elsewhere), `ntdllHandleTracker`/`SearchHandleMap`/`Searches` per-handle state (Eidos has its own kernel-driven inode + opendir-snapshot model — a structurally different but complete solution to the same "stable enumeration / handle->path" problem).

GENUINELY MISSING (no VFS equivalent):
1. MODULE-PATH SPOOFING / inverse tree. usvfs's NtQueryInformationFile(FileNameInformation), NtQueryObject(ObjectNameInformation), GetModuleFileName rewrite a handle's reported path BACK to the virtual path. Under Eidos this is a NON-ISSUE for path reporting (the mount IS at the game Data dir, so a DLL at <mount>/SKSE/Plugins/foo.dll genuinely lives there from Wine's view — no spoof needed). This gap is effectively already closed by the mount topology, EXCEPT where a tool/plugin compares its own reported module path against an expected location; low risk, validated working.
2. TOOLS-THROUGH-VFS RE-ENTRY. usvfs's CreateProcessInternalW injects the DLL into tools (xEdit/FNIS/BodySlide) launched FROM MO2 so they see the same merged view and write back into it. Eidos gets the game's own children for free (namespace inheritance), but a SEPARATELY launched tool from the GUI is in a different namespace and sees the bare game dir. Re-entering the existing mount namespace (via setns on the running game's ns, or re-running the same union) is unbuilt. This is the real gap.
3. PER-CALL SKIP LISTS. usvfs lets MO2 exclude file suffixes / directories. Eidos applies no such filter. Mostly absorbed at layer-build time in Eidos's model (you just don't add a layer), so low priority.

whatEidosShould build:
The headline finding: do NOT port the hooking layer. It is an artifact of intercepting above Wine; Eidos intercepts below Wine, so ~25 of usvfs's ~30 hooks (all the per-call path rewriting, attribute queries, directory merges, INI/move/copy redirection) are already delivered by the existing FUSE union + Wine's own NT->host-syscall translation. eidos-core + eidos-fuse are a complete, correct replacement for the path-interception MECHANISM. This subsystem is therefore NOT a master piece to build — it is a master piece Eidos has ALREADY built by a different route, and this study's value is confirming that and isolating the three true residuals.

Concretely:
1. TOOLS-THROUGH-VFS RE-ENTRY (the one real gap, belongs in eidos-launch + eidos-gui). When the GUI launches xEdit/FNIS/BodySlide, it must run them inside the SAME merged view, not the bare game dir. usvfs does this by DLL-injecting tools spawned from MO2. Eidos's equivalent is namespace re-entry: either keep the game's mount namespace alive and `setns(CLONE_NEWNS)` into it to launch the tool, or (simpler) re-run `launch()` with the identical LayerStack so the tool gets its own mount of the same union. Add a `launch_tool`/`reenter` path to eidos-launch and wire the GUI "Run <tool>" button to it. This is a genuine master-piece-adjacent feature for tool users and is currently unbuilt. Track it as the priority follow-up.
2. MODULE-PATH SPOOFING: explicitly verify, then document as not-needed. Because Eidos mounts AT the game Data dir, a DLL's reported path is already its virtual path; the inverse tree usvfs needs has no analog. Add a regression note (and ideally one integration check that a plugin querying its own module path sees the mount path). No code likely required.
3. PER-CALL SKIP LISTS: defer. In Eidos's model exclusion happens at layer-assembly time (eidos-instance decides which dirs become layers); a per-call suffix/dir filter is a nice-to-have only if a specific game needs to hide a path that is physically present in a layer.

Also fold into eidos-core the two already-tracked correctness items this study reinforces: directory rename across the lower boundary (usvfs models it as copy+delete — adopt the same), and the eventual in-memory resolver index to replace per-lookup `ci_lookup` real-FS stats (usvfs's shared-memory RedirectionTree is the proof that an in-RAM index, not repeated stat()s, is the scalable design for 1000+ mod stacks).
recommendation: Do not build a hooking layer or port any individual usvfs hook. eidos-core's LayerStack + eidos-fuse together are already a complete, behavior-equivalent replacement for usvfs's path-interception mechanism, because Wine translates every NT/Win32 path call into a host syscall that lands on the FUSE mount — so NtCreateFile/NtOpenFile/NtQueryAttributesFile/NtQueryDirectoryFile/GetFileAttributes/MoveFile/CopyFile/GetPrivateProfileString/FindFirstFile are all covered implicitly. The MutExHookGroup re-entrancy guard, GetLastError preservation, device-file/hid# filtering, and per-handle search-state tracking are Windows-in-process artifacts with no FUSE equivalent and no need. (2) Confirm + document that module-path spoofing (usvfs's inverse tree / GetModuleFileName / NtQueryObject reverse-rewrite) is unnecessary because Eidos mounts at the game Data dir, with one integration check. (3) Defer per-call skip lists (handled at layer-assembly time in eidos-instance). Separately, treat usvfs's shared-memory RedirectionTree as confirmation that the planned in-memory resolver index in eidos-core (replacing per-lookup ci_lookup stat()s) is the right scaling design for large load orders.

subsystem: In-memory redirection tree / virtual-path resolution index (usvfs RedirectionTree + TreeContainer vs Eidos LayerStack resolver)
whatMo2Does:
usvfs resolves every virtual path through a pre-flattened in-memory tree, never stating the real FS on the hot path.

DATA STRUCTURE (directory_tree.h). `DirectoryTree<NodeDataT>` node = { TreeFlags m_Flags (DIRECTORY/DUMMY/CREATETARGET); WeakPtrT m_Parent, m_Self; StringT m_Name; NodeDataT m_Data; NodeMapT m_Nodes }. For redirection, NodeDataT = RedirectionData = a single `StringT linkTarget` (redirectiontree.h:46-64) - the absolute real backing path (e.g. the mod's copy of the file). m_Nodes is a boost multi_index `mimap<StringT, NodePtrT, CILess, ...>`: an ordered_unique index whose comparator CILess (directory_tree.h:185) is `_strnicmp(a,b,min(len))` - i.e. the case-insensitivity is BAKED INTO the index ordering, so a lookup is a single case-folding map probe, no per-entry scan.

POSITION-INDEPENDENCE. Children are held by `bi::shared_ptr<NodeT, VoidAllocatorT, DeleterT>` and the whole thing is allocated through `OffsetPtrT` = `bi::offset_ptr<T,int32,uint64>` (shared_memory.h:31). Offset pointers store deltas, not absolute addresses, so the identical tree image is valid in every process that maps the segment at a different base.

RESOLUTION (directory_tree.h:527 findNode). Pure component-by-component descent: `m_Nodes.find(component)` -> recurse into child -> at the last component return the node. Cost = O(depth x log(fanout)) map probes, ZERO filesystem syscalls. The per-API-call entry point is RerouteW::create (maptracker.h:393-442): canonicalize the incoming NT path, `table->findNode(lookupPath)`, and if the node has a non-empty linkTarget (or is a directory) return that real path as the reroute buffer. That string is what the hooked NtCreateFile/NtOpenFile is rewritten to.

PRE-FLATTENING / LAYER PRIORITY. The tree already holds the merged winner per path. addFile -> addNode (tree_container.h:253) inserts with overwrite=true by default, so a later insert REPLACES m_Data.linkTarget (last-writer-wins). MO2 drives this in load order: UsvfsConnector::updateMapping (usvfsconnector.cpp:213) iterates the resolved mapping list and calls usvfsVirtualLinkDirectoryStatic(src,dst, LINKFLAG_RECURSIVE) per enabled mod (usvfs.cpp:716); the recursive walk (usvfs.cpp:742-803) enumerates each mod's real tree ONCE at injection and addFile's every file. So a 110-mod stack is collapsed, before the game starts, into one tree where each virtual path stores exactly one linkTarget = the highest-priority mod that has it. Intermediate dirs are auto-created as FLAG_DUMMY nodes (tree_container.h:281).

SHARED MEMORY (tree_container.h). TreeContainer wraps the tree in managed_windows_shared_memory (a named segment in the pagefile) so the GUI process AND every hooked game/child process share ONE resolved index - build once, read everywhere. Growth: when an insert throws bi::bad_alloc, reassign() (tree_container.h:480) sets outdated=true on the old segment, creates the next segment ("name_N" -> "name_{N+1}") at 2x size, copyTree()s into it, and refcounts (TreeMeta.referenceCount + interprocess_mutex) decide when the old segment is destroyed. Other processes notice outdated on next get() and walk the _N name sequence to the live segment (findNewerBlock, :528).

READDIR MERGE. Only directory listing touches disk: gatherVirtualEntries (ntdll.cpp:420) findNode's the dir, calls node->find(pattern) over the in-memory children (wildcard match), pushes each child's linkTarget as a VirtualMatch, then addVirtualSearchResult opens the REAL backing dir to fetch stat data, deduping by uppercased name (foundFiles set). A separate inverseTable maps real->virtual for the reverse direction.
whyItMatters: This is the single mechanism that makes a deep load order fast, and it is the literal thesis statement of Eidos. The project's own architecture.md (line 71) sells the design as "no lowerdir wall (mods resolve through an in-memory index, not a kernel layer list)" - that is precisely the usvfs RedirectionTree. Without it, resolution cost scales with (number of layers x path depth) in real syscalls, which is exactly the OverlayFS lowerdir-scaling wall the project was created to escape - just relocated from the kernel into eidos-core. usvfs pays the directory-walk cost ONCE at injection (building the tree) and then every one of the millions of path probes a modded game fires during load is a few in-memory map lookups. Eidos currently pays a multi-layer directory scan on EVERY probe. On the validated 110-mod Skyrim run it works, but every lookup/getattr/open/readdir is doing N_layers worth of read_dir scans; this is the property most likely to fall over as load orders or asset counts grow, and the one a knowledgeable user will benchmark against MO2 first. Building it converts "aspirational" (the word the docs use) into the real differentiator.
eidosCurrentState: No index exists; resolution stats the real FS per call. eidos-core/src/lib.rs `LayerStack` holds `layers: Vec<PathBuf>` + `overwrite` and nothing else; `Eidos::new` (eidos-launch/src/lib.rs:108) stores the Vec verbatim with no pre-scan. resolve_read (lib.rs:102) does `self.layers.iter().find_map(|l| ci_lookup(l, vpath))`. ci_lookup (lib.rs:293) walks each path component, tries an exact-case join, and on ANY miss falls back to `fs::read_dir(current)` + linear scan with eq_ignore_case. So resolving one D-deep path that lives in the lowest layer costs up to N_layers x D `read_dir` syscalls; hidden_by_whiteout adds another find_whiteout (a read_dir) per ancestor component; list_dir read_dirs every layer. The FUSE daemon calls these fresh on every operation: lookup (fuse lib.rs:417), getattr (:437), open (:356), readlink (:445), and dir_snapshot->list_dir (:276). What IS cached: the Inodes table (path<->ino, fuse lib.rs:82) and the resolved fd on an OpenFile (so reads after open don't re-resolve, lib.rs:480). Resolution results themselves are never memoized, and there is no cross-process sharing (each per-launch daemon is one process; tools re-entering the namespace would rebuild from scratch). The behaviour is correct and well-tested (18 unit tests) - it's purely the performance/architecture property that's missing.
eidosGap: 1) No tree/index type at all - resolution is a live filesystem walk, not a map descent. 2) Layers are not pre-merged: usvfs collapses the stack to one winner-per-path at build time; Eidos re-derives the winner by scanning layers in priority order on every single lookup. 3) Case-insensitivity is re-done per call via read_dir scans on a miss, instead of being baked into the index key ordering (usvfs's CILess multi_index). 4) No shared/persistent index, so re-entering the namespace to run a tool (xEdit/FNIS) would rebuild resolution from cold FS scans. 5) No equivalent of the DUMMY-node / pre-built directory skeleton, so even directory existence checks scan. Eidos does have things usvfs lacks here (real whiteouts for COW deletes, an Overwrite layer that shadows the index), so the index must be a *merge-on-build* structure that still consults the overwrite layer + whiteouts dynamically, not a verbatim port.
recommendation:
Build the in-memory resolution index in eidos-core as a new module (e.g. `index.rs`) owned by `LayerStack`, replacing the per-call ci_lookup FS walk. Concretely:

STRUCTURE: a case-folded path trie. Node = { children: BTreeMap<String(lowercased key), Node> or HashMap; winner: Option<{ real_path: PathBuf, layer_idx: usize }>; is_dir: bool; cased_name: String (preserve winning layer's casing for readdir/NTFS sort) }. This mirrors usvfs DirectoryTree.m_Nodes (CILess map) + RedirectionData.linkTarget exactly, minus shared memory.

BUILD: on Eidos::new / mount, walk each layer ONCE from lowest priority to highest (or highest-first and skip-if-present) and insert every file/dir, last-writer-wins per node so the highest-priority layer's real_path lands as `winner` - this is the addNode(overwrite=true) + load-order-iteration pattern from tree_container.h + usvfsconnector.cpp:213. One walkdir per layer at startup amortizes all later probes. Cost is the same total read_dir work MO2 does at injection, paid once.

RESOLVE: resolve_read becomes overwrite-layer check (still dynamic, it's COW and mutates at runtime) -> whiteout check -> index.find(vpath) returning winner.real_path. find() is a component-wise BTreeMap descent with the lowercased component as key: O(depth x log fanout), zero syscalls - matching findNode (directory_tree.h:527). list_dir for the mod layers becomes "enumerate the trie node's children" (NTFS-sorted, which you already do) merged with the live overwrite dir.

KEEP THE OVERWRITE LAYER DYNAMIC: do NOT index the overwrite layer - it changes during the run (COW writes, whiteouts). Index only the immutable mod+game layers; consult overwrite + whiteouts live (cheap: one stat of one dir). This is the key adaptation over usvfs, which has no separate writable union layer.

INCREMENTAL UPDATES: provide insert/remove on the index so runtime create/unlink/rename mutate it (usvfs does this via addFile on CreateFile and removeFromTree on delete, maptracker.h:158/189), keeping the index coherent without a rebuild.

LATER (not v1): for tools-through-VFS, persist or rebuild the index per re-entry; a shared-memory/mmap'd form (usvfs's TreeContainer) is only needed if multiple Eidos processes must share one index, which the per-launch model mostly avoids. Skip the doubling/outdated/reassign machinery (tree_container.h) - that exists only because Windows SHM is fixed-size; a Rust process heap grows for free.

VALIDATE: add a bench over the real 110-mod Skyrim Data tree (resolve N random deep paths) showing constant-ish time vs the current N_layers x depth scan, and assert the index produces byte-identical winners to the current resolve_read across the existing 18 unit tests (run both, compare) so the refactor is provably behaviour-preserving.

subsystem: Directory enumeration merge (NtQueryDirectoryFile vs FUSE readdir): ordering, de-duplication, case folding, wildcard matching
whatMo2Does:
usvfs intercepts NtQueryDirectoryFile / NtQueryDirectoryFileEx (src/usvfs_dll/hooks/ntdll.cpp:520-830) and merges two streams per directory handle, tracked in a per-handle Searches::Info (foundFiles set, virtualMatches queue, currentSearchHandle).

ORDER = REAL-FIRST, VIRTUAL-SECOND, NOT globally sorted. The hook first calls the real ::NtQueryDirectoryFile via addNtSearchData() and emits those records verbatim, THEN drains queued virtual matches via addVirtualSearchResult(). The inline comment (ntdll.cpp:528-536, 684-692) states this is deliberate: "if we don't add the regular files first, '.' and '..' wouldn't be in the first search result of wildcard searches which may confuse the caller."
- Real entries: usvfs does NOT re-sort them. It returns whatever order the underlying FS driver gives. On NTFS that is UTF-16 binary (upcased) collation; on FAT/network it is effectively insertion order. usvfs inherits the kernel's order.

The gaps are subtle and mostly favor Eidos, but four are worth recording:

1. SORT SEMANTICS DIVERGE FROM TRUE NTFS, AND THE COMMENT OVERSTATES IT. Eidos sorts by to_ascii_lowercase() then Rust String Ord (bytewise on the lowercased copy). True NTFS collates by UPPER-cased UTF-16 code units (LCMapStringW invariant, the same fold usvfs uses for dedup). For pure-ASCII letters these agree. They DISAGREE on: (a) digits/symbols interleaved with letters -- e.g. '_' (0x5F) sorts AFTER uppercase letters but BEFORE lowercase, so upcase-collation places '_' differently than lowercase-collation; (b) any non-ASCII name (accented, CJK), where ascii-lowercase is a no-op and Rust falls back to raw UTF-8 byte order rather than UTF-16 upcased order. So Eidos is "sorted and deterministic" (which is what actually fixed the crash) but it is NOT byte-identical to what an NTFS volume would have produced. The code comment calling it "NTFS-style" / "Emulate NTFS" is slightly aspirational.

2. EIDOS GLOBALLY SORTS; usvfs DOES NOT. This is a genuine behavioral difference. usvfs returns real-unsorted-then-virtual-sorted; Eidos returns one fully-sorted list. Eidos's behavior is arguably BETTER (more like a real NTFS volume, which is fully sorted) and is what boots the Creation Engine -- but it means Eidos is not bug-for-bug compatible with usvfs, and any game that somehow depended on usvfs's quirky two-block order (none known) would differ.

3. DEDUP WINNER IS OPPOSITE. usvfs returns the REAL-disk copy as the survivor at enumeration; Eidos returns the HIGHEST-LAYER copy (mod over game). Eidos's choice is the correct one for preserving the winning layer's exact casing in the returned name; usvfs gets away with returning the real copy only because the redirected file is physically present in the iterated dir. whatMo2Does:
usvfs has NO internal "overwrite" object. The write destination is a node flagged FLAG_CREATETARGET (usvfs.h LINKFLAG_CREATETARGET, value 0x4) in the redirection tree. MO2 wires exactly one create-target: the Overwrite dir, mapped onto the game Data dir (organizercore.cpp:2140 sets `createTarget = customOverwrite.isEmpty()`; usvfsconnector.cpp:226 passes LINKFLAG_CREATETARGET|LINKFLAG_RECURSIVE to usvfsVirtualLinkDirectoryStatic). Mod dirs are linked WITHOUT the flag, so they are read-only.

Write decision (maptracker.h, class CreateRerouter::rerouteCreate, ~line 551): it calls the *hooked* GetFileAttributesW (so it sees the merged virtual view), maps the NT disposition (FILE_CREATE/OVERWRITE_IF/etc) to a Win32 one (ntdll.cpp:1227-1250), then for a creation it runs the FindCreateTarget visitor up the ancestor chain (ntdll.cpp:210, maptracker.h:536) to find the innermost create-target node and rewrites the path to `node.linkTarget / make_relative(node.path, lookupPath)`. New files get "fake" parent dirs materialised in the overwrite (createFakePath, tracked in k32FakeDirTracker) and a fresh node inserted into the tree (insertMapping -> redirectionTable().addFile). Deletes are virtual: k32DeleteTracker remembers the deleted vpath, the tree node is removed (removeMapping), and a later create is "rerouted to the location of the deleted file".

Virtual-vs-passthrough decision: a path is skipped entirely if interestingPath() rejects it (\\.\ device prefixes, hid#, line maptracker.h:333) or isDeviceFile() (\Device\..., ntdll.cpp:283) or callContext is inactive; otherwise findNode() in the redirection tree decides - a hit returns the linkTarget (virtual), a miss passes the original path through untouched. Skip lists (skipFileSuffixes, skipDirectories in sharedparameters.h) and FAILIFSKIPPED apply at LINK time, pruning what enters the tree (e.g. .git, .mohidden) - they are not consulted per-syscall.

DLL/module handling (the crux): (1) hook_LoadLibraryExW (kernel32.cpp:141) reroutes the path via RerouteW::create then calls the real LoadLibraryExW with the REAL backing path - the DLL loads from its real mod-store location. (2) hook_GetModuleFileNameW (kernel32.cpp:1396) is the key: after the real call returns the real backing path, it runs RerouteW::create(..., inverse=true) against the INVERSE redirection table to translate the real path BACK to the virtual path, so a plugin asking its own path (GetModuleFileNameW(hSelf)) sees `...\Data\SKSE\Plugins\foo.dll`, not the mod-store path. Buffer-size handling re-queries with a growing buffer. (3) Forced libraries (sharedparameters ForcedLibrary list; usvfs.cpp:420 in InitHooks does LoadLibraryExW per entry at injection): a per-process list MO2 exposes as 'Force Load Libraries', used for proxy/inject DLLs (ENB, ReShade, some script-extender shims) the game won't load on its own.
whyItMatters: Write redirection to a single Overwrite target is the absolute core of a mod manager: it is what keeps the game install and every mod source byte-for-byte pristine while still letting the game write saves, INIs, and plugin configs. Without it the manager is just a read-only overlay. The DLL self-path behavior matters because script-extender plugins (SKSE/F4SE and the CommonLibSSE-NG ecosystem) routinely call GetModuleFileName/GetModuleHandleEx on themselves to locate sibling config/data next to their own DLL, and engines/anti-cheat sometimes validate module paths; if the reported path diverges from where the plugin 'should' live, plugins mislocate their assets or refuse to run. Forced libraries are how a whole class of graphics/injection mods load at all.

whatMo2Does:
MO2's install pipeline lives in `InstallationManager::install()` (installationmanager.cpp:624). Flow: (1) read sidecar `<archive>.meta` for Nexus metadata (gameName/modID/version/category); (2) `m_ArchiveHandler->open()` the archive via its bundled 7z wrapper (zip/rar/7z/fomod/001), with a password callback; (3) build a lazy `ArchiveFileTree` (archivefiletree.h) over the archive entries WITHOUT extracting - a tree of FileTreeEntry/IFileTree nodes mapping 1:1 to archive members; (4) collect all `IPluginInstaller` plugins, sort DESC by `priority()`, and try each whose `isArchiveSupported(tree)` is true. Two installer kinds: IPluginInstallerSimple (gets the tree, mutates it to express the desired layout, returns it) and IPluginInstallerCustom (handles the file itself). The first installer to return RESULT_SUCCESS wins; RESULT_MANUALREQUESTED falls through to manual installers; RESULT_NOTATTEMPTED continues the loop.

Key trick: installers don't move bytes. A simple installer rearranges the IFileTree (descend into a top folder, drop junk, set destinations). MO2 then calls `ArchiveFileTree::mapToArchive()` which walks the (possibly reorganized) tree and FLAGS exactly which archive entries to extract and to what output path. `doInstall()` (line 483) then calls `testOverwrite()` (merge/replace/rename/backup dialog if `mods/<name>/` exists), `extractFiles()` extracts ONLY flagged entries straight into the final `mods/<name>/` dir, copies any installer-created files, and writes `meta.ini` (gameName, modid, version, category, installationFile, repository, author, installedFiles array). Extraction runs on a QtConcurrent thread with progress/file callbacks.

THREE installer tiers matter for a clone:
1. **installer_quick** ("Simple Installer", priority 50): the workhorse for ~most Nexus archives. `getSimpleArchiveBase()` recursively descends: at each level, if `ModDataChecker::dataLooksValid(tree)` is VALID (or it looks like a data/text top layer), use that as the mod root; else if the level has exactly ONE subdir, descend into it; else fail. This strips the ubiquitous "ModName-1234-1-0/" wrapper folder so Data-relative files land correctly. If `dataLooksValid` returns FIXABLE it routes to manual/`fix()`.
2. **ModDataChecker** (game feature, moddatachecker.h): `CheckReturn{INVALID,FIXABLE,VALID} dataLooksValid(tree)` + `fix(tree)`. The Gamebryo impl (gamebryomoddatachecker.cpp) declares static sets - valid top-level FOLDERS {meshes, textures, scripts, interface, sound, music, video, seq/strings, skse/obse/f4se/nvse/fose, materials, fonts, menus, CalienteTools, NetScriptFramework, dllplugins, SkyProc Patchers, MCM, ...} and valid file SUFFIXES {esp, esm, esl, bsa, ba2, ini, modgroups}. VALID if any top entry matches; INVALID otherwise. This is the entire 'is this a real Skyrim mod' heuristic.
3. **installer_fomod** (priority 110 if preferred else 90, so it beats Simple): the scripted XML installer. `findFomodDirectory()` locates a `fomod/` dir (descending through single wrapper folders), and `isArchiveSupported` requires `fomod/ModuleConfig.xml`. install() pre-extracts only ModuleConfig.xml + info.xml + every image (buildFomodTree/appendImageFiles), parses ModuleConfig.xml into a wizard, lets the user choose, then `updateTree()` rewrites the IFileTree to contain only the selected files at their destinations.

The FOMOD ModuleConfig.xml engine (fomodinstallerdialog.cpp/.h) is the deep part. Data model: install steps -> groups (GroupType: SelectExactlyOne/AtMostOne/AtLeastOne/Any/All -> radio/checkbox/forced UI) -> plugins (options), each plugin has m_Files (FileDescriptor: source, destination, priority, isFolder, alwaysInstall, installIfUsable), m_ConditionFlags (name=value flags set when selected), and a PluginTypeInfo (default PluginType Required/Optional/Recommended/NotUsable/CouldBeUsable, possibly overridden by DependencyPatterns). Conditions form a tree: SubCondition{operator AND/OR, children} over FileCondition (a plugin file is Active/Inactive/Missing), ConditionFlag/ValueCondition (a flag set by an earlier selection equals X), VersionCondition (game/script-extender/FOMM version >= X). subsystem: Profiles (per-profile mod state, load order, INIs, saves) and how switching a profile re-points the VFS inputs
whatMo2Does:
A profile in MO2 is a directory `<base>/profiles/<name>/`; its name IS its folder name (Profile::name() returns m_Directory.dirName(), profile.cpp:169; rename = QDir::rename, profile.cpp:1018). A profile OWNS, on disk:
- `modlist.txt` - the per-profile enabled-state AND priority. Format: one line per mod, `+Name` (enabled), `-Name` (disabled), `*Name` (foreign/unmanaged DLC), `#` comments. Written in REVERSE priority order (doWriteModlist, profile.cpp:243-281); read back and inverted so highest-priority wins (refreshModStatus, profile.cpp:391-582). `overwrite` is implicit (always last/highest, hasAutomaticPriority).
- `plugins.txt` + `loadorder.txt` + `lockedorder.txt` - the ESP/ESM plugin order (separate from mod order).
- `archives.txt` - BSA list for archive invalidation.
- The game INIs, copied IN at profile creation: `skyrim.ini`, `skyrimprefs.ini`, `skyrimcustom.ini` under the CONFIGURATION ProfileSettings flag via gamePlugin->initializeProfile() + copyToProfile() (copies from My Games / game dir only if absent, else touches empty). `initweaks.ini` is the merged INI-tweaks output (createTweakedIniFile, profile.cpp:283).
- `settings.ini` - per-profile flags via QSettings: LocalSaves, LocalSettings, AutomaticArchiveInvalidation, and a [forced_libraries] array.
- optionally a `saves/` directory when LocalSaves is on.
Crucially, mod enabled/priority state lives ONLY in the profile (m_ModStatus vector rebuilt per-profile in refreshModStatus); the mods themselves in mods/ are GLOBAL and shared across all profiles - profiles differ only by which subset is enabled and in what order. Create-a-copy = copyDir of the whole profile folder (createPtrFrom/copyFilesTo, profile.cpp:729-740). renameModInAllProfiles (profile.cpp:317) rewrites a mod's line in EVERY profile's modlist.txt.
Switching profiles: OrganizerCore::setCurrentProfile (organizercore.cpp:553) constructs a new Profile from the chosen dir, calls m_ModList.setProfile(), applies that profile's archive-invalidation, persists the choice via setSelectedProfileName(), then refreshDirectoryStructure(). The VFS inputs are rebuilt entirely from the active profile by fileMapping(profileName) (organizercore.cpp:2070): it iterates profile.getActiveMods() (priority-ordered enabled dirs) into source->target mappings, appends localSaves->mappings(profile/saves) to redirect the game's save dir into the profile (organizercore.cpp:2122), appends the global overwrite dir, then plugin mappers. So a profile switch = re-read modlist.txt + re-point saves + re-point INIs, then re-feed usvfs.
whyItMatters: Profiles are the feature that lets one mod collection serve many playthroughs/configs: a heavy graphics build vs a vanilla-plus build vs a testing sandbox, each with its own enabled set, load order, INIs and (optionally) saves, all sharing the same downloaded mods on disk. It is one of the top reasons people use MO2 over Vortex, and it is what makes safe experimentation possible (toggle 40 mods off in a new profile without touching your main). For Eidos to be a credible MO2 replacement rather than a single-config mod launcher, multiple profiles are expected baseline functionality. It is also a natural prerequisite for the planned plugin-load-order/LOOT and per-game-INI work, since in MO2 those artifacts are profile-scoped by design - building them flat now would mean reworking them later.

subsystem: ESP/ESM/ESL plugin load-order management (PluginList model + plugins.txt/loadorder.txt persistence + LOOT sorting)
whatMo2Does:
MO2 keeps the plugin load order in a dedicated Qt model, `PluginList` (modorganizer/src/pluginlist.h/.cpp, ~2185 lines), entirely SEPARATE from the mod-folder order. It scans the VIRTUAL data dir (the merged view) for *.esp/.esm/.esl, and for each builds an `ESPInfo` by parsing the TES4 header via `ESP::File`: isMaster (header flag 0x01), isLight (flag 0x200, ESL), isMedium (Starfield ESH), isBlueprint, hasNoRecords (dummy), formVersion, headerVersion, author, description, and the MAST subrecords = its masters (pluginlist.cpp:2127-2180).

Two distinct integers per plugin (pluginlist.h:343-345): `priority` (contiguous 0..N, the user-facing order, persisted) and `loadOrder` (the game-visible index, -1 if disabled). `syncLoadOrder()` walks plugins in priority order and assigns loadOrder only to enabled ones (pluginlist.cpp:906-918). `generatePluginIndexes()` computes the hex mod-index the game/console uses (pluginlist.cpp:1281-1326): normal plugins get a 2-hex sequential index; ESL/light get `FE:xxx` (254 + numESLs/4096, 3-hex slot); Starfield medium/ESH get `FD:xx` (253 + numESHs/256). Three "fix" passes enforce the rules every refresh: `fixPriorities()` compacts priorities; `fixPrimaryPlugins()` pins the game's primary masters (Skyrim.esm etc.) to the top in canonical order; `fixPluginRelationships()` forces ALL masters above ALL normal plugins, blueprint masters into their own block, and every master before its dependents (pluginlist.cpp:343-456). `setPluginPriority`/`changePluginPriority` re-enforce these constraints on drag-reorder so you cannot drop a master below its child or an esp above an esm (pluginlist.cpp:1940-2016).

Persistence is delegated to a per-game feature `GamePlugins` (uibase .../game_features/gameplugins.h): `writePluginLists`/`readPluginLists`/`getLoadOrder`, plus capability flags lightPluginsAreSupported / mediumPluginsAreSupported / blueprintPluginsAreSupported, and the game declares a `LoadOrderMechanism` (FileTime vs textfile/asterisk vs None). The gamebryo implementation writes two files into the game's local AppData: loadorder.txt (full order, UTF-8) and plugins.txt (System encoding). For modern games (Skyrim SE/VR, Fallout 4, Starfield) the asterisk format is used: a single plugins.txt where ACTIVE plugins are prefixed with `*`; older games (Skyrim LE, FO3/FNV) use plain plugins.txt = active set + loadorder.txt = full order; Oblivion/Morrowind use file mtimes (`saveLoadOrder` sets FILETIME = (145731+priority) days, pluginlist.cpp:812-867).

LOOT integration (modorganizer/src/loot.cpp, loot.h, lootdialog.cpp): MO2 does NOT call libloot in-process. `runLoot()` saves the current plugin list, spawns the bundled `loot/lootcli.exe` INSIDE the usvfs (so LOOT sees merged plugins) with args `--game <lootGameName> --gamePath <dir> --pluginListPath <profile>/loadorder.txt --out lootreport.json --pluginListOutputPath loadorder.txt --language ...` (loot.cpp:462-507). It streams progress/log lines over a named pipe (`\\.\pipe\lootcli_pipe`) parsed by lootcli::parseMessage, shows a `LootDialog` with a markdown report (QWebEngine), then parses lootreport.json into per-plugin reports (dirty/ITM, missing masters, incompatibilities, messages, Bash tags) attached to rows via `addLootReport`, and applies the sorted order from the output loadorder.txt through `PluginList::setLoadOrder`. The masterlist/userlist (LOOT's metadata, fetched from loot/skyrimse etc. git repos) are handled by lootcli/libloot, not MO2; MO2 just passes `--skipUpdateMasterlist` when it already updated.
whyItMatters:
For every Bethesda Creation-engine game (Skyrim, Skyrim SE, Fallout 3/NV/4, Oblivion, Morrowind, Starfield, Enderal - exactly Eidos's catalog), the MOD-FOLDER order (which loose file wins) and the PLUGIN order (which .esp/.esm record wins, and which gets which FormID modindex) are two independent axes, and BOTH must be correct or the game is broken. Eidos's FUSE union solves only the first axis. The second is non-optional: with the wrong plugin order or unsatisfied masters the game crashes on load (a plugin loaded before its master = instant CTD), and with no plugins.txt management a 110-mod load order is unusable.

Concretely, a real Skyrim SE setup has ~150 plugins; nobody orders them by hand - LOOT is the de-facto standard sorter and the reason MO2/Vortex are usable at scale. Today Eidos validated that the 110-mod FILES load and SKSE DLLs run, but it has no control over plugins.txt, so the active set and order are whatever the prefix already contained. The moment a user adds/removes a plugin-bearing mod, they have no way to activate it, order it, or sort it. This is the difference between "merges files" and "is a mod manager."

whatMo2Does: MO2 builds ONE in-memory merged tree that stores winner AND losers at every file node. DirectoryRefresher::refresh() (directoryrefresher.cpp) creates a root DirectoryEntry, seeds game data as origin 0, sorts enabled mods by priority ascending (prio = modlist index + 1), then walks each mod's files (one ModThread per mod) via addFromOrigin into the shared tree. Each leaf FileEntry (fileentry.h) holds a single primary m_Origin (winner OriginID) plus m_Alternatives, an AlternativesVector = vector<FileAlternative{OriginID, DataArchiveOrigin}> (all losers). FileEntry::addOrigin() arbitrates incrementally: if the incoming origin's FilesOrigin priority beats the current winner's (or a loose file supersedes an archived one) it pushes the old winner into alternatives and makes the newcomer the winner; otherwise it inserts the newcomer into alternatives at its priority slot. FileEntry::sortOrigins() finalizes order (loose by FilesOrigin priority, archive by BSA load order, loose beats archive). A FilesOrigin (filesorigin.h) is one mod/data-dir/BSA: {id, name, path, int priority, set<FileIndex>}. Per-mod flags come from ModInfoWithConflictInfo::doConflictCheck() (modinfowithconflictinfo.cpp): per file it reads getOrigin() vs getAlternatives() to fill six std::set<unsigned int> of mod indices (overwrite/overwritten + archive + archive-loose), derives EConflictType (NONE/OVERWRITE/OVERWRITTEN/MIXED when both sets non-empty/REDUNDANT when the mod has visible files but wins none), and emits EConflictFlag values for the mod-list icons; the Conflicts struct is memoized (MemoizedLocked) and invalidated on refresh. Display: GeneralConflictsTab (modinfodialogconflicts.cpp) bins a mod's files into Overwrite/Overwritten/No-conflict trees; AdvancedConflictsTab shows the before/after origin chain; the Data tab (filetreemodel.cpp) sets FileTreeItem::Conflicted when alternatives is non-empty and labels the winning mod.
whyItMatters: Conflict resolution is THE day-to-day reason MO2 exists. Across 50-110 mods, many files (meshes, textures, scripts, skeleton.nif, animation behaviors) are provided by several mods at once and which one wins decides whether the game looks/behaves right or breaks. The modder constantly asks: which mod overwrites this file, what am I losing, is this mod fully redundant, should I reorder. MO2's winners/losers data plus red/green/mixed flags and the Conflicts tab are the primary tool for that, and it is the single most-used diagnostic in the app. A replacement that only says 'highest-priority wins' (no losers, no per-mod flags) cannot explain WHY the merged view looks as it does. subsystem: Game launch: process construction, environment/PATH, working directory, and process-tree lifetime (MO2 spawn.cpp + processrunner.cpp + usvfs injectProcess/forceLoad vs eidos-launch)
whatMo2Does:
MO2's launch path is `ProcessRunner::runBinary` -> `spawn::startBinary` -> `spawn::spawn` (spawn.cpp:419). It builds the command line as `"\"<bin>\" <args>"`, sets CWD to the executable's working dir (which defaults to the binary's own dir, and for the game is the game root; processrunner.cpp:560-567), and calls `usvfsCreateProcessHooked(...)` (the hooked variant) with flags `CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB` (spawn.cpp:458). Five distinct env/process behaviors:

(1) PATH APPEND (the task's explicit question): immediately before CreateProcess, `env::appendToPath(QDir::toNativeSeparators(moPath))` appends MO2's OWN applicationDirPath to %PATH% (env.cpp:390: `set("PATH", old + ";" + s)`), then restores it right after with `env::setPath(oldPath)` (spawn.cpp:448,471). WHY: confirmed from usvfs inject.cpp:94-140 + usvfs.cpp:817-859 + usvfs_proxy/main.cpp. The usvfs runtime DLL (`usvfs_x64.dll`) and `usvfs_proxy_x64.exe` live in MO2's install dir. When the hooked game later spawns a CHILD process, usvfsCreateProcessHooked re-injects usvfs into that child via `usvfs::injectProcess(dllModule's parent dir, ...)`; the proxy and DLL are found relative to the module dir, but PATH-on-the-spawning-process is what lets the loader resolve the usvfs DLL by name in edge cases (and lets helper.exe/proxy resolve siblings). It is explicitly NOT for the game's own DLLs - those are served by the VFS. The append is scoped to MO2's own process env for the duration of the CreateProcess call only.

(2) SteamAPPId env var: `checkSteam` always does `env::set("SteamAPPId", steamAppID)` (or the global settings app id) before launch (spawn.cpp:618-622), so the game's steam_api(64).dll initializes against the right app without a steam_appid.txt; it also detects steam_api(64).dll in the game dir to decide whether Steam must be running, and can launch Steam.exe via the HKCU\Software\Valve\Steam\SteamExe registry value.

(3) CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB so the child is not trapped in any job MO2 inherited, enabling MO2 to put it in its OWN job for monitoring.

(4) FORCED LIBRARIES: per enabled ExecutableForcedLoadSetting, `usvfsForceLoadLibrary(processName, libraryPath)` (usvfsconnector.cpp:285-295) stores (processName, libraryPath) pairs in usvfs shared memory (SharedParameters::addForcedLibrary, sharedparameters.cpp:231). On injection, InitHooks runs INSIDE the target and calls `context->librariesToForceLoad(exePath.filename())` - a CASE-INSENSITIVE match on the exe BASENAME - then LoadLibraryExW's each matching path from within the process (usvfs.cpp:418-433). This is the ENB/proxy-DLL mechanism (force-load a mod's d3d11.dll/dxgi.dll into SkyrimSE.exe).

(5) PROCESS-TREE WAITING: spawned handles are added to a `CreateJobObjectW` job (processrunner.cpp:365-401); a worker thread (`waitForProcessesThreadImpl`, :284) repeatedly calls `env::getProcessTree(job)`, recursively finds the most 'interesting' non-hidden leaf (skipping ModOrganizer.exe/conhost.exe; findInterestingProcessInTrees, :135), waits on it with exponential backoff (50ms..2000ms), and loops until the whole tree drains. This survives launcher chains (Bethesda/Steam launcher -> game, or skse64_loader.exe -> SkyrimSE.exe) and keeps the VFS connected until every descendant exits. Also note `adjustForVirtualized` (processrunner.cpp:13-55): if the binary/CWD is under mods/, MO2 re-launches a second ModOrganizer.exe with a `launch <cwd> <bin> <args>` command so the tool runs inside the same VFS (the 'tools-through-VFS' re-entry).
whyItMatters: Three of these five matter for a usable Linux replacement; two do not. (a) CWD=game-root: Eidos ALREADY does this and correctly documents the load-bearing reason (CommonLibSSE-NG's relative versionlib path). (b) Process-tree lifetime is the one that bites real launchers: under Proton the chain is reaper -> wine -> launcher -> game, and if Eidos's daemon were torn down when the FIRST child returns, a launcher that exec-hands-off to the game would drop the union mid-game. (c) The PATH-append and usvfs-DLL injection are Windows-NT-hooking artifacts with NO Linux analog: Eidos virtualizes via a FUSE mount the child already sees, so there is nothing to inject and no usvfs DLL to put on PATH. The SteamAppId/Steam-launching logic is also mostly handled FOR Eidos by Steam itself when launched as `eidos play <id> -- %command%`. The genuinely missing capability is FORCED LIBRARIES (ENB/proxy DLLs like d3d11.dll, dxgi.dll, .asi loaders): on Windows MO2 force-injects them; on Linux the equivalent is WINEDLLOVERRIDES plus making sure the override DLL is visible in the merged view at the game root - and Eidos sets no env at all today.

Concretely missing for parity, in priority order:

1. FORCED LIBRARIES has no equivalent at all. LaunchSpec has no field for proxy/override DLLs and launch() sets no env. The Linux-correct mechanism is: (a) ensure the override DLL (e.g. a mod's d3d11.dll) wins in the merged view at the game root [Eidos resolution already handles this if the mod ships it], and (b) set WINEDLLOVERRIDES=d3d11=n,b (or the right token) so Wine loads the native/builtin override. Eidos sets no WINEDLLOVERRIDES, so ENB/ReShade/.asi-style mods that depend on DLL override cannot work even if the file is present in the union.

2. PROCESS-TREE LIFETIME is single-child only. `cmd.status()` waits on the forked PID. If that PID is a launcher/loader that re-execs or spawns the real game and exits, `drop(session)` unmounts WHILE the game is still running. Under Proton the immediate child is usually the long-lived wine process so this has worked for the 110-mod test, but it is fragile for any launcher that detaches (Bethesda launcher, some SKSE/script-extender setups, or Steam's own reaper handing off). There is no analog to MO2's job-object tree-drain.

3. NO ENV CUSTOMIZATION HOOK. 4. NO per-executable working-directory override: launch() hardcodes CWD=game_root. MO2 lets each Executable carry its own workingDirectory (processrunner.cpp:560-567); a tool like BodySlide may need its own CWD.

recommendation:
Do NOT chase PATH/DLL-injection parity - those are NT-hooking artifacts with no Linux meaning; Eidos's FUSE-mount-the-child-already-sees model makes them moot, and the task's literal question ('why does MO2 append its own dir to PATH') resolves to: to let the loader find usvfs_x64.dll / usvfs_proxy_x64.exe when re-injecting child processes - irrelevant to Eidos. Instead, in eidos-launch/src/lib.rs:

(1) Add an `env: Vec<(String,String)>` (and optionally `cwd: Option<PathBuf>`) field to LaunchSpec, and apply it via `cmd.envs(&spec.env)` (and `cmd.current_dir` override) before `cmd.status()`. This is a ~10-line, low-risk change that unlocks both forced-libraries and tools-through-VFS env.

(2) Build forced-libraries ON TOP of (1) as a thin helper: given a list of override DLL stems the user enabled, compose/append `WINEDLLOVERRIDES=stem1=n,b;stem2=n,b` (merging any inherited value) into spec.env. The DLL file itself is already served by the union if a mod provides it. This is the honest Linux equivalent of usvfsForceLoadLibrary and is what makes ENB/ReShade/.asi mods viable. Model the data shape on MO2's ExecutableForcedLoadSetting (process basename + library path + enabled).

(3) For process-tree lifetime: today's single `cmd.status()` is adequate for the validated Proton path but should be hardened. The right Linux primitive is a PID namespace (CLONE_NEWPID) so the forked child is PID 1 of its own namespace and the kernel reaps the whole tree when it exits, OR a cgroup/`prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER)` + drain loop. Recommendation: add CLONE_NEWPID to the existing unshare in launch() (it composes with CLONE_NEWNS) and wait for the PID-1 child; this is the closest analog to MO2's job-object tree-drain and prevents premature unmount on launcher hand-off. Treat this as a separate, carefully-tested change because PID-ns + Proton interaction needs validation.

The reason a tool sees the SAME mods as the game is the usvfs architecture, NOT anything tool-specific: usvfsCreateVFS() (usvfsconnector.cpp) runs ONCE at MO2 startup and creates a NAMED shared-memory VFS, instance name SHMID="mod_organizer_instance". The redirection/virtual-mapping tree lives in that managed_shared_memory segment (tree_container.h createSHM/openSHM by name, auto-growing to a renamed 2x segment when full). The VFS is process-lifetime, not per-launch. Each launch only rebuilds the mapping: OrganizerCore::beforeRun() -> UsvfsConnector::updateMapping() -> usvfsClearVirtualMappings() + usvfsVirtualLinkDirectoryStatic/usvfsVirtualLinkFile for the current load order, reusing the same SHM. To put a process into that view, ProcessRunner -> spawn::spawn() calls usvfsCreateProcessHooked() (usvfs.cpp:817): CreateProcessW with CREATE_SUSPENDED, then usvfs::injectProcess() injects the usvfs DLL; the DLL's InitHooks() does `new HookContext(*params)`, which ATTACHES to the same named SHM via params->instanceName, then ResumeThread. The standalone re-entry primitive is usvfs_proxy/main.cpp: `--instance <SHM>` opens the named segment bi::open_only, then either injects into an existing `--pid` or spawns a new `--executable` suspended + injects + resumes. processrunner.cpp adjustForVirtualized() additionally rewrites a tool whose binary/cwd lives under mods\ to its virtual game\data\ path and relaunches through MO, so tools shipped inside a mod resolve in the virtual tree. Output of a tool lands in Overwrite (or a per-executable custom_overwrites mod), and afterRun() refreshes the directory structure so the game then sees what the tool generated.
whyItMatters: The entire point of a Skyrim/FO4 mod manager is the generate-then-play loop: FNIS/Nemesis build FNIS_*.hkx and the behavior files from the installed animation mods; BodySlide builds meshes from the installed bodies/outfits; xEdit cleans masters and makes merged/conflict-resolved patches; Wrye Bash builds a Bashed Patch; the Creation Kit reads the full load order. whyItMatters:
For a Bethesda-game MO2 replacement (Eidos's validated target - Skyrim SE, Fallout 4, etc.), three of these features are not optional polish - they are the difference between mods loading and the game ignoring them, and crucially they are all realized THROUGH the VFS, which is exactly Eidos's layer:

1. GamePlugins + the plugins.txt/loadorder.txt mapping: a Bethesda game reads its active ESP/ESM set and load order from %LocalAppData%/<game>/plugins.txt + loadorder.txt. MO2 generates these from the user's order and VFS-maps them into place. Eidos currently mounts the union over Data but never produces or places these files, so a modded ESP load order is simply not communicated to the game. Eidos's 110-mod Skyrim test works because SKSE DLLs (loose files under Data/SKSE/Plugins) load purely from the Data union - but that test does NOT exercise ESP plugins, which is most of real modding.

2. BSAInvalidation + DataArchives: Bethesda engines prefer files packed in vanilla BSAs over loose files unless invalidation is active (bInvalidateOlderFiles=1 + dummy BSA + empty SInvalidationFile). Many mods ship BSAs that must be added to SResourceArchiveList to load at all. Without this, a large class of texture/mesh/sound mods silently do nothing even though the union serves their files correctly.

3. documents-dir INIs + LocalSavegames: per-profile INIs (skyrim.ini/skyrimprefs.ini) and isolated saves are core MO2 value (try a load order without polluting your main game; INI tweaks like uGridsToLoad). Under Proton these live in compatdata/<appid>/pfx/drive_c/users/steamuser/Documents/My Games/<game>/ - reachable from Linux, so implementable.

The ScriptExtender feature is the launch entry point itself: you must run skse64_loader.exe, not the vanilla launcher. Eidos already hardcodes this swap (see Eidos gap), proving the per-game need is already biting.

The declarative basic_games schema matters because it is how MO2 scaled to ~80 games with near-zero code per game - the right shape for Eidos's catalog to grow.

whatMo2Does:
MO2 has two layers: the InstanceManager owns instance discovery/selection, and ModInfo owns per-mod metadata.

INSTANCE LAYOUT (appconfig.inc, instancemanager.cpp, settings.h::PathSettings): A "global" instance is a folder under AppData/Local/ModOrganizer/<InstanceName>/; a "portable" instance lives in the app directory itself and is detected purely by the presence of ModOrganizer.ini, with a portable.txt lock file forcing portable mode. Each instance owns a single ModOrganizer.ini plus the directories mods/, overwrite/, downloads/, profiles/, webcache/, logs/, crashDumps/. The INI is the source of truth for which game the instance manages: GameSettings reads [General] gameName + gameEdition (variant) + selected_profile, [Settings] base_directory, and [Paths] mods/downloads/overwrite/profiles/cache (each resolvable via the %BASE_DIR% token so the whole instance is relocatable). Instance::setup() reads the INI, resolves the game plugin by case-insensitive gameName (falling back to "which plugin says this directory looksValid()"), then writes any missing values back (updateIni). objectsForDeletion() enumerates exactly the owned dirs+INI for safe deletion. Load ORDER is NOT at instance level: modlist.txt lives per-PROFILE under profiles/<name>/, alongside plugins.txt/loadorder.txt/local INIs/saves.

PER-MOD META (modinforegular.cpp readMeta/saveMeta): every managed mod is a folder mods/<Name>/ containing meta.ini, a flat QSettings INI. Keys: gameName, modid (Nexus id, -1 if none), version + newestVersion + ignoredVersion (parsed VersionInfo), installationFile (the archive it came from), category (comma-joined integer category IDs, first = primary), repository (default "Nexus"), author/uploader/uploaderUrl, url + hasCustomURL, comments/notes/color, endorsed (int tri-state enum), tracked (bool), converted/validated (flags to silence wrong-game / invalid-data warnings), nexusDescription/nexusFileStatus/nexusCategory, and three timestamps lastNexusQuery/lastNexusUpdate/nexusLastModified (ISO-8601). Plus an [installedFiles] array of (modid,fileid) pairs, an [INI Tweaks] array, and a [Plugins] group for plugin-scoped key/values. Meta is written lazily (only when m_MetaInfoChanged) and flushed in the destructor.

UPDATE-CHECK + PROVENANCE: updateIndices() builds s_ModsByModID[(gameName, modid)] from the meta. updateAvailable() = installed version < newestVersion (or non-active Nexus file status). checkAllForUpdate() gathers the distinct gameName set and the min/max lastNexusUpdate, then picks the cheapest Nexus API path (per-game bulk updates vs per-mod), throttling by API budget. The download sidecar .meta (downloadmanager.cpp createMetaFile, an INI next to the archive) carries gameName/modID/fileID/version/name/modName/repository/category/author/uploader; on install these fields are copied into the mod's meta.ini, so a mod always knows where it came from and what file it was.
whyItMatters: meta.ini is the single highest-leverage piece for turning Eidos's anonymous mod folders into a managed, MO2-migratable library: it is the only enabler of update checks, categories, and provenance, and it is a stable on-disk format that existing MO2 instances already populate, so round-tripping it unlocks zero-friction migration.
eidosCurrentState: eidos-instance/src/lib.rs is a deliberately minimal model: Instance { root } with helpers mods_dir()/overwrite_dir()/base_dir(), a global path of $XDG_DATA_HOME/eidos/<game-id>, a portable variant at an explicit folder, and modlist() / save_modlist() / load_order() that read+write modlist.txt (lines prefixed + enabled / - disabled, top = highest priority; folders missing from the file are appended enabled, vanished entries dropped). That modlist.txt + COW overwrite/ design is sound and already validated end-to-end on a 110-mod Skyrim SE run. But: there is NO per-mod metadata of any kind (a grep across every .rs file in crates for meta.ini/category/nexus/version/provenance/endorsed returns zero hits), NO instance manifest INI (the managed game id is implicit in the directory name, never written down), NO profiles/ directory (load order lives at instance root, not per-profile), and NO downloads/ concept. The game id that would seed both the instance path and the meta gameName field comes from eidos-games::GameDef.id (e.g. "skyrimse").
eidosGap:
Three concrete gaps, in priority order:
1. No per-mod meta.ini equivalent. Eidos cannot record or read version, nexus modid, category, installation file, endorsed/tracked, or converted/validated for any mod. This blocks update checks, categorization, and provenance entirely, and blocks importing existing MO2 instances (whose mods/<Name>/meta.ini files Eidos currently ignores).
2. No instance manifest. The instance does not persist its game id, schema version, or selected profile; it is inferred from the path. Fine for global instances, fragile for portable ones and for forward-compat.
3. No profiles or downloads model. MO2 keeps modlist.txt/plugins.txt/loadorder.txt/INIs/saves per profile; Eidos keeps a single modlist.txt at root. Profiles are a separate (nice-to-have) master piece; downloads ties into the future installer/Nexus work.
recommendation:
Build the per-mod meta layer in eidos-instance now; it is a true master piece and the highest-leverage non-FUSE work left. Concretely:

1) Add a `ModMeta` struct + read/write in eidos-instance (new module meta.rs), persisted as `mods/<Name>/meta.ini`. KEEP MO2's exact key names and INI shape so existing MO2 instances round-trip unchanged: gameName, modid, version, newestVersion, ignoredVersion, installationFile, category (comma-joined int IDs, first = primary), repository, author, uploader, uploaderUrl, url, hasCustomURL, comments, notes, endorsed, tracked, converted, validated, lastNexusQuery/lastNexusUpdate/nexusLastModified (ISO-8601). Use the `rust-ini` crate (handles the flat-key + groups + array-ish layout) and SemVer-tolerant version parsing matching MO2's VersionInfo. Treat all fields as optional with MO2's defaults (modid = -1, repository = "Nexus"). Defer the [installedFiles] array, [INI Tweaks], and [Plugins] group to a v2 - they are not needed for update checks or categorization.

2) Hang meta off ModEntry: add `meta: ModMeta` (lazily loaded) to the struct returned by modlist(), and a save_meta() that writes only when dirty (mirror MO2's m_MetaInfoChanged so you never rewrite untouched files and never clobber MO2's extra keys - preserve-on-read-and-merge). Seed gameName from eidos-games::GameDef.id.

3) Add a thin `update_available(meta)` = version < newestVersion helper now (pure, unit-testable), and an `(game_id, nexus_id)` grouping fn, so the future Nexus crate only has to fill newestVersion. Do NOT build the Nexus HTTP client here.

4) Add a minimal instance manifest `eidos-instance.ini` at the instance root: schema_version, game_id, (optional) selected_profile. Write it in Instance::create(); read it to recover the game id instead of inferring from the path. This is small and unblocks portable instances + forward-compat.

5) Categories: store the raw integer IDs in meta (MO2-compatible) but ship Eidos's own category-id to name table as data (a static map, MO2 ships categories.dat); do not require the Nexus category import. Surface categories as a filter column in eidos-gui later.

Leave profiles/ and downloads/ as separate follow-ups (profiles = its own master piece; downloads pairs with the installer). The instance INI and meta.ini both belong in eidos-instance, consumed by eidos-gui and eidos (CLI).

Provenance chain: download sidecar <archive>.meta (downloadmanager.cpp createMetaFile) stores gameName/modID/fileID/version/name/modName/repository; on install these copy into the mod's meta.ini

Update-check: updateIndices() builds s_ModsByModID keyed on (gameName, modid); checkAllForUpdate() buckets by distinct gameName + min/max lastNexusUpdate to pick bulk-vs-per-mod Nexus API; updateAvailable() = installed version < newestVersion
category key = comma-joined integer category IDs, first element is the primary category; resolved against a CategoryFactory id->name table
converted/validated booleans exist purely to suppress wrong-game and invalid-data warnings; endorsed is an int tri-state (TRUE/FALSE/NEVER), tracked is bool
Instance INI (ModOrganizer.ini): [General] gameName/gameEdition/selected_profile, [Settings] base_directory, [Paths] mods/downloads/overwrite/profiles/cache with %BASE_DIR% token for relocatability
Portable vs global: portable = ModOrganizer.ini present in the app dir (+ portable.txt lock forces it); global = subfolder under AppData/Local/ModOrganizer/<name>/
Load order is per-PROFILE (profiles/<name>/modlist.txt + plugins.txt + loadorder.txt + local INIs/saves), NOT at instance level
